name: Grace Okafor

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Grace. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or any party. Everything you tell me is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Could you start by telling me a bit about yourself?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Grace, I'm 27, and I drive an electric rope shovel at an open-pit copper mine. It's the big digger that loads the haul trucks, with a bucket you could park two cars in. I'm lead operator on my crew, so I train the new shovel drivers and sort out the loading plan with the pit supervisor. I live with my girlfriend Ana in a two-bedroom unit in town; she teaches maths at the high school.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And what does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Twelve-hour shifts, four on and four off, days then nights. I climb up into the cab, do my checks, and then I'm loading trucks every two or three minutes for most of the shift, reading the dig face and keeping the floor flat so the trucks don't bog. I love it when the rock's broken well and I can fill a truck in four passes. What wears me out is night shift in winter, and drivers who park badly and cost me a minute every load.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: I'm going to describe five pictures of the future, one at a time. The first is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay. That's a pretty comfortable picture for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, now let's talk about the stuff that actually matters, like fatigue on twelve-hour nights and housing costs in town. Everyone's been so distracted by AI that nobody's fixed the camp food. I'd probably post something like that, half joking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be relieved. Copper's in demand for all the electric cars and power lines, so the pit has a long life ahead. My job would feel about as safe as a job can feel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I'm doing and push for my next step, maybe pit supervisor in a few years. I'd keep putting money aside, I've got about four months saved, and Ana and I want a deposit for a house. I might use one of those chat tools now and then to help write my supervisor application, like I did for my last review.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty settled. Glad, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about your work or money that worries you even in that picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rent's gone up twice in two years because the mine keeps bringing in contractors and they all need housing. That's the thing that bugs me. It's not scary, just annoying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would becoming a supervisor change for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: More money, fewer night shifts, and a say in how the crew is run. I'd be the first woman supervising in our pit, and I won't pretend that doesn't matter to me.

say: The real issues are **fatigue** on night shifts and **housing costs** in town.
AI talk has **distracted everyone** from fixing ordinary things like camp food.
think: Copper demand for **electric cars** gives the pit a long life.
Her job would feel **as safe as** a job can feel.
do: Keep running the shovel and apply for **pit supervisor** in a few years.
Keep saving towards a **house deposit** with her partner Ana.
Use a **chat tool** now and then to help write applications.
S0.quote: Copper's in demand for all the electric cars and power lines, so the pit has a long life ahead.
fieldNote: She's confident because of **copper demand**, not because she ignores technology.
**Rising rent** from contractor housing is her only real gripe here.
Becoming the **first woman supervisor** in her pit clearly matters to her.

steps.text: Apply for pit supervisor within a few years
Keep saving for a house deposit with Ana

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, that one feels close. We've already got some of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say we need the union at the table before every new system comes in, not after. Our mine is already trialling driverless haul trucks on the east ramp. I'd say publicly that workers should share in the savings, not just the shareholders.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, reading a dig face is hard, so the shovel is one of the last machines they'll automate. But the planning side is going to software fast. The dispatch and the loading plans go first, so the supervisor job I want might shrink before I get there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the mine to put me on the remote-operation course they run for the truck controllers, so I understand the new systems. I'd join the union's technology committee, because someone my age should be on it. And I'd keep saving, maybe a bit more than now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy. Not for my job this year, more for where it's all going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about in that picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The truck drivers, especially the ones on the east ramp. A few of them are older guys who came over from farming. Leroy, a driver I trained with, has already asked me whether he should do a forklift ticket, just in case.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use more AI tools yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the mine gave us a tool for planning loads, I'd try it once someone else had tested it. I'm not going to be the first, but I'm not going to be the last either.

say: The **union** should be at the table **before** each new system arrives.
Workers should **share the savings** from automation, not just shareholders.
think: The shovel is among the **last machines** to be fully automated.
**Planning and dispatch** go to software first, so the supervisor job may shrink.
do: Ask for the mine's **remote-operation course** to learn the new systems.
feel: **Uneasy** about where it's heading, not about her job this year.
S1.quote: Reading a dig face is hard, so the shovel is one of the last machines they'll automate. But the planning side is going to software fast.
fieldNote: She separates **hands-on digging** from the planning work she hopes to move into.
Worry runs first to the **truck drivers**, already seeing driverless trials.
**Steady** style: she'll try tools once others have tested them.

steps.text: Take the mine's remote-operation course for truck controllers
Raise monthly savings towards the house deposit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2028? That's basically tomorrow in mining time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say loudly that this is a political choice, not a weather event. If machines do the work, the profits need to be shared through tax and a proper safety net. I'd be posting about it, going to rallies, the lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, by 2031 a robot shovel could do what I do. I'd be 32, with a technical diploma for a job that doesn't exist. The mine would buy the robot the day it's cheaper, and that's the bit that scares me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd push my savings from four months to six and put the house deposit on hold. I'd try to get into the remote operations centre, because someone will still need to watch the robots for a while. And I'd be heavily involved in the union's campaign for redundancy terms and a robot tax.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick in my stomach. Like the rug's been pulled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Ana decide about the house?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd wait. Ana's job is probably safer than mine, but neither of us wants a mortgage on one income in a mining town where the mine's just let everyone go. That's a horrible thought, actually, because we've been planning it for two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the shovel would be one of the last to go. Does that still hold with three years' warning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It buys me maybe those three years, that's all. The planning part goes in 2028 with the thinking AI, so the supervisor job's gone first. Then the hands-on part goes in 2031.

say: Mass automation is a **political choice**, not a weather event.
Profits should be shared through **tax** and a proper **safety net**.
think: A **robot shovel** could do her job by 2031.
At 32 she'd hold a **diploma** for a job that no longer exists.
do: Raise savings from four to **six months** and pause the **house deposit**.
Try to get into the **remote operations centre** to watch the robots.
Campaign through the union for **redundancy terms** and a robot tax.
feel: **Sick** in her stomach, like the rug has been **pulled**.
S2.quote: By 2031 a robot shovel could do what I do. I'd be 32, with a technical diploma for a job that doesn't exist.
fieldNote: She sees the job going in **two steps**: planning in 2028, digging in 2031.
Pausing the **house plan** with Ana hit her hardest.
Turns fear into **political action** quickly and confidently.

steps.text: Build savings from four to six months
Apply for a role in the remote operations centre
Campaign through the union for a robot tax
Put the house deposit with Ana on hold

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Still fast, but there's some room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have a few years and no excuse to waste them. I'd push for the company and the government to fund retraining now, while people are still earning. That's the message I'd put out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think it means my shovel job runs to about 2034, and that the supervisor job I want shrinks around 2031. So I've got time to switch, but not a lot. I'd need to pick something that robots and AI won't take straight away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd look into training as a mine safety inspector with the state regulator, because I think governments will still want a person signing off. I'd do that course part-time over the first couple of years. Ana and I might still buy, but something small, with a deposit we can afford if I'm out of work for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but I can see a path. That makes a big difference.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why a safety inspector?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because when something goes wrong in a pit, people want a human to blame and a human to trust. I've seen a wall fail, I know what it looks like. That's worth something to a regulator, I hope.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave town for that job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, the regional office is two hours away in the city. Ana could teach there easily. We'd miss the people here, but we're young and we haven't got kids yet.

say: There are a few years and **no excuse** to waste them.
Firms and government should fund **retraining now**, while people still earn.
think: Her shovel job runs to about **2034**; the supervisor job shrinks by 2031.
She has **time to switch**, but not much.
do: Study part-time to become a **mine safety inspector** with the regulator.
Consider a **smaller house** with a deposit that covers time out of work.
S3.quote: When something goes wrong in a pit, people want a human to blame and a human to trust.
fieldNote: She picks a **regulator job** because she thinks people will still want a human to sign off.
Her **real experience** of a wall failure is the asset she leans on.
Willing to **move cities** because there are no kids yet.

steps.text: Study part-time for a mine safety inspector role
Move two hours to the regulator's city office
Buy a smaller house with a deposit that leaves a buffer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. Okay, I can breathe with that one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the version where we can actually get it right, if we start now. Unions, councils and the mines should be planning together. I'd want my union to have a ten-year plan, not a press release.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd still lose the shovel by about 2039, when I'm 40. That's mid-career, which isn't great. But ten years is enough to become a supervisor, then move into the regulator side, and have money behind me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go for supervisor in the next couple of years, as I'd planned anyway. Then I'd start the safety inspector study around year four or five. Ana and I would buy the house, and I'd try to pay it down hard before the robots arrive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer. Still a bit of a knot, but it feels like a career plan instead of an emergency.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said ten years is enough. What could still go wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The mine could automate early to save money, before 2039. Or the regulator might use AI for inspections too. I'm guessing, honestly. Nobody really knows.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to the new shovel drivers you train?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the new shovel drivers to get a second ticket early, electrical or diesel, and to save from day one. I wish someone had told me that at nineteen.

say: Ten years is the version where we can **get it right**.
Her union should have a **ten-year plan**, not a press release.
think: She'd still lose the shovel around **2039**, at age 40.
Ten years is enough to supervise, move to the **regulator**, and save.
do: Go for **pit supervisor** in the next couple of years.
Start **safety inspector** study around year four or five.
Buy the house with Ana and **pay it down** hard.
feel: **Calmer**, like a **career plan** rather than an emergency.
S4.quote: I'd tell the new shovel drivers to get a second ticket early, electrical or diesel, and to save from day one.
fieldNote: Even with ten years she expects to **lose the shovel job** mid-career.
She **admits uncertainty** about whether the regulator path is safe.
Advice to trainees shows she thinks in **crew terms**, not just her own.

steps.text: Apply for pit supervisor within two years
Start safety inspector study around year four
Buy the house with Ana and overpay the mortgage

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. It's the speed. We'd have no time to put rules in place, and the mine would just do whatever saves money. What would help is a law that makes companies fund retraining and redundancy before they automate, and a regulator that actually has people on it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about being a woman in this job. I fought hard to get on the shovel, and losing it to a machine just when women are finally getting senior roles feels unfair. Nobody talks about that.

headlineQuote: I fought hard to get on the shovel, and losing it to a machine just when women are finally getting senior roles feels unfair.
portrait: A 27-year-old **lead shovel operator** at an open-pit copper mine, living with her partner Ana, a maths teacher.
Progressive and union-minded; she calls mass automation a **political choice** and wants profits shared.
Sees her job going in two steps: **planning work** first, then digging when robots arrive.
Plans a move into **mine safety inspection** with the regulator as her long-term path.
Calm only in AI Plateau; the **house plans** with Ana bend with each faster scenario.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because there'd be no time to put rules in place.
whatWouldHelp: A law making companies fund **retraining and redundancy** before they automate.
A regulator with **real people** on it.
